summary.text: A 12-year-old boy of non-consanguineous parents had anemia and intermittent hemoptysis since age four, DAH treated for eight years with glucocorticoids/immunosuppressants and relapses, then relative stability before one day of viral symptoms. He required continuous oxygen; examination showed dyspnea and suprasternal retraction without rales. Mild anemia, neutrophilic leukocytosis, mild PCT elevation and hypoxemia contrasted with normal CRP. H1N1 sequences were 59,806 in nasopharyngeal swab and 7,570 in BALF, with initial GGO and septal thickening.

Oral baloxavir 40 mg once and IV methylprednisolone 2 mg/kg/day gave only slight dyspnea improvement at two weeks. Dyspnea then persisted despite continuous oxygen; Hb was normal on repeat. Sudden worsening revealed massive left pneumothorax and worse CT abnormalities. Drainage resolved pneumothorax but lung changes persisted, prompting nintedanib for suspected viral-associated lung injury/fibrosis.

After two months of nintedanib dyspnea improved but intermittent oxygen was still needed. Nintedanib was withdrawn for unspecified social/personal reasons; oxygen was successfully withdrawn three months later. Later CT and captioned five- and six-month scans partly improved. BALF color versus absence-of-hemorrhagic-BALF claims remain conflicting.

summary.text: A seven-year-old girl of non-consanguineous parents with recurrent unexplained anemia, DAH diagnosed and glucocorticoids started one year earlier, relapses and then relative stability presented after four weeks of dyspnea/cough needing continuous oxygen. Dyspnea, suprasternal retraction and moist end-inspiratory rales accompanied hypoxemia, absent anemia and normal WBC/CRP/PCT.

Initial CT showed diffuse GGO and marked septal thickening; cloudy white BALF tNGS detected only CMV, 735 reads. Suspected viral-associated lung injury/fibrosis was treated with IV ganciclovir; reads fell to 60 at two weeks, followed by another two weeks of treatment. CMV was absent on later six-month BALF testing. Serial captioned CT at one, three and six months and one year showed partial resolution, with acute hemorrhagic manifestations absent in discussion.

summary.text: A nine-year-old girl of non-consanguineous parents had anemia and intermittent hemoptysis since age six, prior CT/BALF hemosiderophage testing, and DAH diagnosed before glucocorticoids begun two months earlier. After relative stability she developed two days of fever, fatigue, cough, congestion and rhinorrhea with HPIV detected at 41,766 reads in nasopharyngeal tNGS. Symptomatic/supportive care was provided because no effective antiviral was available; CT showed diffuse GGO and marked septal thickening.

Dyspnea worsened and required continuous oxygen. Four-week CT after HPIV remained severely abnormal; viral-associated lung injury/fibrosis was considered and later supported by prolonged CT changes. A significant Hb fall supported an alveolar hemorrhage episode. She died four weeks later from bacterial/fungal co-infection despite antibacterial and antifungal drugs.

article_limitations: Figure pixels were inspected at low resolution (757x353, 757x320, 697x198 JPEG montages); panel-to-panel density comparisons depend on slice level and window and are not independent confirmation of captioned findings. Time labels for follow-up panels follow caption order and are not printed on the images.
No explicit same-patient prior-report linkage identified. References are bibliographic, not patient identity evidence.
No numeric doses for nintedanib, ganciclovir, oxygen or unnamed antibacterial/antifungal drugs are stated.
Case 1 BALF colour (dark red-brown, rust-colored) conflicts with the discussion statement that cases 1 and 2 lacked hemorrhagic BALF; literal colours scored, discussion negative review-only.
Follow-up CT months without explicit anchors are not converted to calendar dates or forcibly aligned to drug-course intervals.
Discussion-level statements that "all cases" were immunocompromised and had pre-existing lung injury and fibrosis are collective author assertions applied to each case without per-patient detail.
